Measure Comfort Alongside Every Savings Claim

A heating control can lower use by delivering less heat. That isn't an acceptable saving if bedrooms become uncomfortable. The property team needs a comfort record alongside the energy record before it changes schedules, resets controls or reports results.

Choose representative suites across the building's exposures, including corner units, and place temperature loggers where they capture occupied-room conditions. Pair those readings with outdoor temperature and heating degree days, so a colder spell isn't mistaken for a control failure.

Compare conditions before and after a control change across similar weather. If the building has different orientations or heating zones, don't assume one logger represents every suite. What an Energy Management System Does in a Building

At a 120-suite mixed-use building, the January gas bill jumps while some residents say their bedrooms are cold. A monthly bill shows that the building used more gas, but it can't tell the property manager whether the heating schedule changed, a control failed, or some suites are not getting enough heat.

An energy management system is a repeating cycle of inventory, measurement, analysis, action and review. It combines utility records, meter readings, building conditions and operating decisions, then checks whether the changes improved performance. It isn't a software screen by itself.

Heating is the practical test

Heating is where a Canadian building's energy management work often meets its hardest trade-off: reduce avoidable use without leaving people cold. Natural Resources Canada's 2025–2026 Energy Fact Book reports that space heating accounted for 56% of commercial and institutional building energy use in 2022, with water heating adding 6%. It also notes that fossil-fuel equipment used for space and water heating produced more than 96% of building operating emissions.

That makes a lower energy chart an incomplete result. In the Canadian government research cited in the fact book, data-driven supervisory controls reduced heating energy costs by 22% and greenhouse-gas emissions by 73% without compromising thermal comfort. Cooling-system controls reduced electricity consumption by 19%. The lesson for a property manager is to evaluate both the energy carrier and the conditions residents experience, rather than treating any drop in consumption as success.

A gas-heated building will show heating changes mainly on the gas meter. An electrically heated building, including one with heat pumps, may show them on the electricity meter instead. The same control strategy can therefore affect different readings, and the right measurement depends on the equipment.

A sound system starts with a meter hierarchy, then uses a scorecard, a practical implementation sequence and a comfort check. It also needs safeguards against false savings. If the building needs envelope improvements as well as better controls, this guide to exterior upgrades that help save energy can help owners consider measures that reduce heat loss at the building boundary.

Connect Submeters to Trustworthy Building Data

Benchmarking and savings claims stall when the owner can't assemble one consistent record for the whole building. The Canada Green Building Council identifies standardized whole-building energy data as a foundational gap for benchmarking, emissions verification and sustainable-finance assessments. Before choosing controls or reporting a saving, establish how each meter relates to the utility account and to the loads inside the property.

The Natural Resources Canada energy management guidelines recommend documenting bills and meter readings, accounting for purchased and on-site energy sources, and building a baseline from at least two years of data. The same discipline helps a property team distinguish tenant allocation from whole-building performance.

Build the meter hierarchy

Level What it measures Read type Data owner Interval
Bulk utility meter Whole-site electricity, gas, steam or water on the invoice Measured by utility Account holder Monthly bill, interval where offered
Common-area meter Lobbies, corridors, parking and amenities Measured or estimated Owner Interval where installed
Suite meters Each suite's electricity or heat Measured Owner or billing agent Monthly or interval
Branch meters Domestic water or thermal loops for fan coils, hydronic heat or VRF Measured or estimated Owner or mechanical contractor Interval where installed

For every level, record whether reads are measured or estimated, who maintains the data, and how frequently readings are available. Then reconcile the suite totals and common-area load against the utility invoice each month. If the totals don't align, treat the difference as a data-quality issue to investigate before it becomes a billing dispute.

Use the hierarchy to describe what each meter can prove. Suite readings can support billing and help identify unusual use, but they aren't a public ranking of residents. Common-area readings show the shared loads separately, which makes it easier to tell whether a change came from a suite or from lobbies, parking or amenities. For an overview of how connected meter networks collect and communicate readings, see this explanation of advanced metering infrastructure.

Set rules for interpreting changes

Number the following checks and assign an owner for each:

  1. List every energy source. Record electricity, gas, steam, water and thermal energy in physical and cost units so no carrier disappears from the picture. The usual slip is an electricity-only inventory.
  2. Gather a usable history. Collect monthly records covering at least 24 months, and use interval data when it's available. One unusually mild or cold season can distort a comparison.
  3. Create a normalized baseline. Adjust the reference for weather and operating conditions so a change in use isn't mistaken for better performance. An unadjusted utility bill doesn't make a fair baseline.
  4. Identify significant energy uses. Separate suites, common areas, domestic hot water, HVAC and central plant loads. The common slip is treating tenant allocation as proof of building-wide improvement.
  5. Assign owners and controls. Give each significant use a responsible person, operating controls, a target and an action plan. A target without an owner is easy to ignore.
  6. Review performance regularly. Use dashboards and management reviews to spot deviations and correct them. Waiting until the season ends can leave an operating problem in place for months.

A useful test this month is simple: check whether suite and common-area readings reconcile with the bulk invoice. If a retrofit, vacancy change or fuel switch alters the building, revisit the baseline. Otherwise, an old reference can hide a real improvement or make a normal change look like a saving.

KPIs for a Multifamily Energy Management System

KPI What to record Canadian reference Review
Site energy use intensity Gigajoules per square metre of floor area Median 1.1 GJ/m² across 30,500 benchmarked buildings Monthly and annual
Source energy use intensity Upstream energy per square metre Median 1.3 GJ/m² Annual
Electricity share Percent of reported energy 51% Monthly
Natural gas share Percent of reported energy 40% Monthly
Carrier coverage Electricity, gas and any steam, water or thermal in one inventory Multi-carrier, not electricity alone At setup
Suite versus common split Percent of metered load in suites versus lobbies, corridors, parking and amenities Building-specific, no national median Monthly
Comfort check Indoor temperature band plus heating or cooling complaint count Hold comfort while energy falls Monthly in heating season

Its national benchmarking population covers 30,500 buildings representing 380 million square metres of floor area. The national medians offer a reference point, not a pass-or-fail grade for an individual apartment building.

Read a high result as a question

If a property's weather-adjusted site intensity sits well above 1.1 GJ/m², investigate heating and shared areas before blaming residents. Check whether the floor area is recorded correctly, whether all energy carriers are included and whether a central plant serves spaces beyond the residential suites. A high figure is a prompt to investigate, not a verdict about tenant behaviour.

Site and source intensity answer different questions. Site intensity measures the energy delivered to the building. Source intensity accounts for energy used upstream to supply it. Their difference is a reminder that a property's electricity and gas use can't be treated as interchangeable units when comparing performance.

Electricity and natural gas are separate scorecard rows for a reason. Electricity accounted for 51% of reported consumption in the benchmark, and natural gas for 40%. The national figures don't tell you how much energy goes to suites versus shared spaces. Build that split from the building's own meter records, and review it alongside the comfort pair: a defined indoor temperature band and a count of heating or cooling complaints. Neither metric is enough on its own; together, they help show whether consumption changed while conditions remained acceptable.

A warm winter can make a gas bill look better even when the building's operation hasn't changed. Before celebrating, compare heating use under similar weather conditions and check whether residents remained comfortable. What you see Likely cause Check before reporting
Gas use down after a mild winter Weather, not operations Normalize with heating degree days
Energy down and heating complaints up Comfort was cut Restore the temperature band and recount complaints
Suite total down, house meter flat Cost was reallocated Report suite and common area separately
Utility bill and submeters do not match Estimated read or data gap Reconcile and fill the interval before any claim
Intensity jumps after a retrofit Old baseline still in use Document the change and rebuild the baseline

If gas use falls, normalize for heating degree days before attributing the change to operations. Set expectations with evidence

Natural Resources Canada's guidance on the ISO 50001 energy management standard reports that Canadian companies implementing ISO 50001 achieved an average cumulative energy-performance improvement of nearly 10% within the first two years.
